questions.topic: The halving distance of a decay curve

answer.exemplar: The decline is produced by three separate frictions, and they are worth separating because they respond to different remedies. The first is the generalised cost of moving: fares, fuel, time and the inconvenience of the journey, all of which rise with distance, so a trip that has to be made becomes more expensive and more tiring the further it goes. The second is the number of chances to interact. If contacts arise whenever two people are in the same place at the same time, and that chance grows with the size of each of the two populations, then the expected number of contacts is proportional to the product of the two sizes divided by some measure of the space that separates them, which is the form the gravity model takes and of which the decay function is a special case. The third is the search cost of a one-off decision: a firm weighing a supplier, a household weighing a school or a patient weighing a specialist samples only a few alternatives, and a distant one is less likely to enter the sample at all. None of the three is inevitable. A faster connection lowers the generalised cost, and it then pays to concentrate activity so that the shorter journeys are more frequent, which is the same mechanism that produces a city. What the decay describes is a cost imposed on the far end, and it falls on whoever is located there, which is why peripheral locations are disadvantaged in a way that aggregate figures for the whole region conceal.

questions.explanation: The question asks for causes rather than a description of the curve, so the answer has to distinguish three frictions that a single number cannot separate, and then connect the frictions to who pays. A fitted decay constant is a summary of their joint effect, and treating it as a natural law rather than as a summary of costs is what makes it look inevitable.
questions.hint: Separate the cost of moving, the number of chances to meet, and the cost of searching further afield.

answer.exemplar: The semivariance at zero separation should be zero, because a point compared with itself has no difference. A positive value there can only come from differences that persist at arbitrarily small distances, and there are three ordinary sources of them. The first is measurement: every instrument has error, so two readings of the same place differ by a fixed amount that the semivariogram cannot separate from real variation. The second is the sampling design, because a pair recorded as coincident is rarely coincident, and a station or a well sampled twice is really two nearby points. The third is variation at a scale finer than the data can resolve, so the process is not smooth at the scale being studied. The distinction matters because the nugget is the part of the variance an interpolation cannot explain. Where the semivariogram is flat from zero outwards, the nearest samples carry almost no information about the point being estimated, and the best estimate is close to the mean of the data with a large variance attached. Where it rises from a small nugget, nearby samples are genuinely informative. Reporting a kriging variance without the nugget gives a false impression of confidence, because the variance at a sampled point is the nugget and never zero.

questions.explanation: A semivariance is a measure of difference, so a positive value at zero separation is a statement about how much difference the data retain when there should be none. The three sources have different remedies, which is why the cause matters: measurement error is fixed by better instruments, sampling design by more and closer samples, and unresolved fine-scale variation by a study area large enough for the process to be smooth.

questions.explanation: A kriging variance is a prediction variance: it says how far the estimate at that location can be expected to sit from the true value. Its size is governed by the arrangement of the samples and by the semivariogram, not by the spread of the values, so a region with a narrow value range but widely spaced samples can have a large kriging variance, while a region with a wide range and dense samples can have a small one. That is why the same map can be confidently mapped in a well-sampled district and barely mapped at all across a data gap. Two practical consequences follow. First, the variance belongs on the map, because a shaded surface of estimates with no uncertainty layer invites the reader to treat the surface as equally reliable everywhere. Second, at a location that was actually sampled the variance is the nugget rather than zero, because measurement error and micro-scale variation are not removed by the interpolation.

answer.exemplar: A second-order surface adds terms for the square of each explanatory variable and for the product of the two, so on a map it allows the surface to bend along one axis, to bend along the other, and to tilt differently in the two directions together. When that reduces the residual variation to nothing, the conclusion is specific: the five observations can be reproduced exactly by a quadratic form, so whatever process produced them had a curvature the first-order surface could not represent. It does not follow that the process itself is a quadratic function of position, and it certainly does not follow that the surface will predict correctly at a point that was not observed. With a small number of points and a flexible form an exact fit is close to unavoidable, and a surface that passes through every observation can still be badly wrong between them. The difference between the two fits is a difference in flexibility rather than in truth, and the honest response to a well-fitting quadratic is to ask what a first-order term would have failed to capture, whether there is a mechanism that predicts that curvature, and whether more observations support the bend or contradict it. A residual reduced to nothing is a statement about the data in hand, and a mechanism is what would make it a statement about the place.

questions.explanation: Degree centrality counts the links at a node and divides by the largest number any node could have, which in a network of five is four, so the central settlement scores 4/4 = 1.0 and each outer settlement scores 1/4 = 0.25. answer.exemplar: Two people can meet whenever the time and place where they are coincide, and neither of those is under the single control of either participant. One has to travel to where the other happens to be, so the first limit is the cost of that journey, and a cost of 30 minutes removes an hour from a day for every meeting. Beyond the journey time there is a second limit that matters more: the number of chances to coincide. If a person has a contact with one colleague on one occasion in ten and meets a different colleague on the other nine, then the number of possible contacts grows with the number of people available rather than with effort, and the effective ceiling on a relationship is set by the size and the variety of the pool. That is why a small town can sustain a great many acquaintances and a large city sustains more of them but fewer apiece, and why concentration is not the same as contact. The two limits together are the time-space constraint, and the ways around it are the ways societies loosen it. Transport changes the journey cost. Telephony removes the need to coincide at all for many purposes. A larger or more varied pool of people changes the number of chances without anyone moving. Working hours change when the day can contain a meeting at all, since a journey only helps if there is time to make it. Each of these shifts the constraint without relocating anybody, which is why the geography of interaction changed sharply while the map of where people live stayed much the same.

questions.explanation: The question is about the two limits that hold interaction down, and the useful move is to separate the cost of a journey from the sheer number of chances two people have of meeting. The second limit is the one that a change in transport alone does nothing about, and it is what makes the size and variety of a place matter rather than only its speed of travel.
questions.hint: Consider both the cost of travelling and the number of chances two people have of being in the same place.

questions.explanation: The shape needs three different causes, because no single one produces a slow start followed by a fast middle followed by a slow finish. Early on, most people have not seen the innovation and cannot evaluate it, so the rate is limited by how fast information spreads at all. In the middle, two feedbacks work together: an adopter has something to demonstrate, and demonstration is cheaper than advertising, and an adopter also reduces the risk for everyone else, so each adoption lowers the cost of the next. At the end, the remaining people are those for whom the innovation does not fit, so the pool is progressively less suitable. The consequence for fitting is severe: a straight line through the early years under-predicts the middle, and a straight line through the middle passes a ceiling the process cannot cross, so a forecast is a claim about the shape of the whole curve.

The cities adopt in order of size as well, so something about the places is at work: a larger city offers more chances of contact, more suppliers who know the method, and a thicker labour market from which to copy. Once both are in play the innovation is not simply spreading outwards, it is spreading through a hierarchy, and a model built on distance alone will get the timing wrong. answer.exemplar: The two schemes optimise different things, and neither is neutral. A scheme that minimises the variation within classes is trying to make each shade on the map as tight a statement as possible, so a reader looking at one colour can infer a narrow range of values. That is the right aim when the map exists to show where the values are genuinely different, and it is the aim behind the natural breaks approach, which searches for the set of boundaries that gives the smallest total within-class variation. A scheme that equalises the number of districts per class is optimising legibility and comparability instead: it guarantees that every shade is used on a known number of units, so a reader can rank the districts and know how many of them are in each group, and it prevents a long tail of extreme values from being given the same status as the bulk. The schemes disagree when the values are not evenly spread, and the disagreement is informative rather than a defect. On a set of eight values that is heavily skewed, the equal-interval scheme yields class sizes of 5, 1, 1 and 1 while the quantile scheme yields 2, 2, 2 and 2, and the quantile scheme has the larger within-class variation even though it looks more orderly. The choice cannot be made from the arithmetic, because it depends on the question the map is meant to answer, and the honest procedure is to state the scheme with the map and, where the distribution is skewed, to show a second classification beside it.

questions.explanation: A classification scheme is an argument about what a shade on a map means, and the two schemes make different arguments: one says a shade stands for a narrow range of values, the other says a shade stands for a known share of the units. The comparison is settled not by the arithmetic but by the question the map has to answer, and the two disagree exactly where the distribution is uneven.
questions.hint: Identify what each scheme holds constant, and then ask what question each is the better answer to.
questions.learningObjective: compare two classification schemes and the questions each answers

The households figure is a red herring and a dangerous one, because allocating by household share would give 0.35 of 48,000, which is 16800, a difference of 9600 people in the one sub-area. That difference is not noise: it is a direct measure of how many more people are in the floodplain during the working day than at night, which is exactly the kind of finding areal interpolation exists to surface. questions.explanation: A pooled rate is a weighted average of the district rates, and the weight is the population, not the number of districts. In the standard version of this pattern the larger district has the higher rate and also holds more people, so the weighted average is pulled towards the larger district and above both district figures even though each district is below the pooled value. The arithmetic makes it unavoidable: if the two rates are 4 and 10 per thousand and the populations are 1,000 and 9,000, the pooled rate is the weighted sum of 4 times 1,000 and 10 times 9,000 divided by 10,000, which is 9.4 per thousand, above both. Nothing is wrong with either district figure and nothing is wrong with the pooled one, but the pooled figure describes no actual place, since it is a property of the pair of districts rather than of anywhere in particular. The remedy is to stop pooling: report the districts, or report small areas so the composition varies less between them.

questions.explanation: The expected number of false positives is the number of tests times the significance level, so 60 tests at 5% gives 3, and simulating 200,000 runs of 60 tests at that level returns a mean of 3.0 with about 95.4% of runs producing at least one false positive. Six significant cells therefore carries no more than three real findings in expectation, and the surplus over three is not obviously a discovery. The correction is standard and cheap, and it takes the form of demanding a stricter level as the number of tests grows, or of reporting how many results were examined. The deeper point is that a map of local tests and a map of one global test answer different questions, and a map dotted with 6 significant cells out of 60 will look like a story about six places when it may be a story about the analysis.

answer.exemplar: The two differ in what the numbers describe. A zonal statistic takes the values belonging to each district and reduces them to one figure per district, so it answers a question about the district: its mean, its total or its share. The reduction is the whole difficulty, because districts differ in size, in how many values they hold, and in the spread of those values, so a large district contributes more to the picture than a small one and a district whose values vary widely can hold a total that overstates how much of the area is affected. A focal statistic takes a single value at a point, the district's own location, so it answers a question about that place: what is the value here. It is the right choice when the phenomenon is genuinely concentrated, as a measurement of air quality at a station or a survey of one household is, and the wrong choice when the average over the district is what matters, since one point cannot represent a spread. The practical consequence is that the two analyses can disagree, and a regional pattern assembled from focal values can look different from one assembled from district averages even with the same underlying data. The choice cannot be dodged by averaging the two: the reduction is not a nuisance to be smoothed, it is a statement about what the map claims, and it has to be stated with the map.

questions.explanation: The distinction is between a summary of everything inside a unit and a value at a point. Both are legitimate, and each answers a different question, so the choice cannot be settled by preferring one as more accurate: it has to be settled by asking whether the phenomenon is concentrated or spread, and then stating the choice with the map so a reader knows what each figure describes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the number describes a place or a summary of the things inside a place.
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a zonal statistic from a focal statistic and their uses

questions.explanation: A Voronoi cell is the set of points nearer one service than any other, and the boundary between two of them is where the two distances are equal, which is a straight line rather than a curve. Setting the squared distance to the second point equal to the squared distance to the third and cancelling the terms leaves 16y equal to 20x minus 36, so the boundary is y equal to 1.25x minus 2.25. At x equal to 4 that is y equal to 2.75, and the household's northing of 5 is above it, placing it on the third point's side, which confirms the direct calculation of 5.00 km against 7.81 km. The same reasoning gives y equal to 4 as the boundary between the first and third points, and the household lies above that too, so it is unambiguously in the third point's cell. The method rests on assumptions that have to be stated: straight-line travel, an unbounded plane, and a demand that does not change across the boundary.

questions.explanation: The difference of 3.15 km, or 0.46%, comes from the flat approximation in the first figure. A degree of longitude is 111.32 km at the equator and shrinks towards the poles in proportion to the cosine of the latitude, so a flat calculation has to apply that cosine, and applying it correctly still leaves a small excess because the flat formula measures a straight line on a plane while the true shortest route bends around the sphere. The size of the error depends on latitude: the same 20 degree separation at 30 degrees north gives 962.98 km by the flat route against 962.67 km, a difference of only 0.30 km. A study of flows should use the shorter figure, because a distance overstatement inflates every gravity prediction built on it, and the effect is worst exactly in the high latitudes where distance matters most.

questions.explanation: The arithmetic is right: 41.2 plus 12.6 minus 33.4 is 20.4, and a third of that is 6.8. What fails is the interpretation. A degree of latitude is close to 111 km everywhere, but a degree of longitude shrinks from 111.32 km at the equator to about 34.6 km at 72 degrees north, so equal steps in longitude are not equal ground distances, and a distance-based average of positions has to be formed on a flat or projected surface where such an average is meaningful. Averaging positions also blurs the sign convention: the third centroid is in the southern hemisphere, and a single mean latitude of 6.8 north says nothing about the fact that one of the three lies below the equator. The defensible alternatives are a mean centre computed from projected coordinates, or a statement about the arrangement itself, such as one district north, one near the equator and one south of it.

questions.explanation: The order matters because each step fixes something the next one depends on. The question and the measure come first, since a count of cases and a rate per head answer different questions and a cluster is defined relative to a population, so stating that early prevents the choice of measure being made to produce a result. The unit of analysis and the neighbour rule come next, and they are the two decisions that most often determine the answer: a district that is treated as adjacent to its neighbours on a map of counties may be adjacent to nothing at all once the zones are smaller. Building and normalising the weights follows from the neighbour rule, since the weights are just that rule written down. The test is last, and repeating it on a second unit of analysis belongs with it rather than after the writing, because a pattern that survives a change of zoning is much harder to explain away as an artefact of the boundaries.
questions.hint: Fix the question and the measure first, then the spatial structure, then the test, then check it twice.

questions.explanation: The first step is checking the samples, because an interpolation reproduces every input faithfully, so a single mis-keyed value is not smoothed away but spread across the cells around it in proportion to its weight. The structure of the spatial variation is settled next, by computing the semivariogram and comparing its sill with the variance of the data: a sill well below the data variance means there is a large-scale trend or an outlier left in the sample, and a semivariogram still rising at the longest separation means the sample is too small to describe the structure. Only then is it worth choosing the estimator and its search neighbourhood, since the weights are derived from that structure. The fit is tested against samples deliberately held out, which is the only check that catches a surface that passes through its inputs and nothing else. The last step publishes the variance with the surface, because an interpolated value without a measure of its uncertainty invites the reader to treat the whole map as equally reliable.
questions.hint: Check the data, establish its structure, choose and test the estimator, then publish with the uncertainty.
